---
title: "minimap"
---






`minimap` provides `purrr`-style mapping functions -- `.iter_map()`,
`.iter_map2()`, `.iter_imap()`, `.iter_walk()`, `.iter_iwalk()`, and the
type-stable `.iter_map_dbl()`/`.iter_map_lgl()`/`.iter_map_chr()` -- built
entirely on `lapply()`/`vapply()`. See the
[README](https://github.com/djnavarro/minis/tree/main/minimap) for the
full API reference and scope notes; this page walks through each one,
starting from the basic case and building up to the two-input and
side-effect variants.

## Functions

### Core functions

- `.iter_map(.x, .f)` -- apply `.f` to each element of `.x`, always
  returning a list, with names preserved.
- `.iter_map_dbl()`/`.iter_map_lgl()`/`.iter_map_chr()` -- like
  `.iter_map()`, but return an atomic vector of the named type instead
  of a list, via `vapply()`.
- `.iter_map2(.x, .y, .f)` -- apply `.f` to corresponding pairs of
  elements from two same-length lists/vectors.
- `.iter_imap(.x, .f)` -- apply `.f` to each element of `.x` together
  with its name.
- `.iter_walk(.x, .f)` -- like `.iter_map()`, but for side effects only:
  returns `.x` invisibly instead of the results.
- `.iter_iwalk(.x, .f)` -- like `.iter_imap()`, but for side effects
  only: returns `.x` invisibly instead of the results.

### Internal helpers

- `.iter_assert(expr, message)` -- a small argument-checking helper
  built on base `stop()`, used to validate inputs like matching
  lengths or the presence of names.

## `.iter_map()`

`.iter_map()` is the workhorse of the mini: apply a function to each
element of a list or atomic vector, and get back a list of results the
same length, with any names from the input preserved on the output.
It's a thin wrapper around `lapply()`, so anything you already know
about `lapply()`'s behaviour carries over directly:




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
.iter_map(1:3, function(x) x + 1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[[1]]
[1] 2

[[2]]
[1] 3

[[3]]
[1] 4
```


:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
.iter_map(c(a = 1, b = 2), function(x) x * 10)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$a
[1] 10

$b
[1] 20
```


:::
:::




Because the return type is always a list, `.iter_map()` is safe to use
even when `.f` returns different types or lengths for different
elements:




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
.iter_map(1:3, function(x) if (x == 2) c(x, x) else x)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[[1]]
[1] 1

[[2]]
[1] 2 2

[[3]]
[1] 3
```


:::
:::




## Type-stable variants

Often you know in advance that every element of the result will be a
single number, logical, or string -- in which case getting a list back
is inconvenient. `.iter_map_dbl()`, `.iter_map_lgl()`, and
`.iter_map_chr()` cover that case: they behave like `.iter_map()`, but
return an atomic vector of the named type via `vapply()`, which also
means they *validate* that every call to `.f` really does produce a
length-1 value of the expected type:




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
.iter_map_dbl(1:3, function(x) x + 1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2 3 4
```


:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
.iter_map_lgl(1:5, function(x) x %% 2 == 0)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE
```


:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
.iter_map_chr(c(a = 1, b = 2), function(x) sprintf("value is %s", x))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
           a            b 
"value is 1" "value is 2" 
```


:::
:::




If `.f` breaks that promise -- by returning a vector of length 2
instead of 1, say -- the call errors immediately rather than silently
producing a malformed or recycled result:




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
.iter_map_dbl(1:3, function(x) c(x, x))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error}

```
Error in `vapply()`:
! values must be length 1,
 but FUN(X[[1]]) result is length 2
```


:::
:::




## `.iter_map2()` and `.iter_imap()`

Sometimes one input isn't enough. `.iter_map2()` walks two same-length
vectors in parallel, calling `.f` with one element from each:




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
.iter_map2(1:3, 4:6, function(x, y) x + y)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[[1]]
[1] 5

[[2]]
[1] 7

[[3]]
[1] 9
```


:::
:::




Passing vectors of mismatched length is a deliberate error rather than
silent recycling:




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
.iter_map2(1:3, 1:2, function(x, y) x + y)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error}

```
Error:
! `.x` and `.y` must have the same length
```


:::
:::




`.iter_imap()` covers a related but different need: walking a single
named vector together with its own names, rather than a second vector.
`.f` is called with the element first, then its name:




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
.iter_imap(c(a = 1, b = 2), function(val, name) paste0(name, "=", val))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$a
[1] "a=1"

$b
[1] "b=2"
```


:::
:::




`.x` must actually be named for `.iter_imap()` to make sense, and that's
enforced:




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
.iter_imap(1:3, function(val, name) paste0(name, "=", val))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error}

```
Error:
! `.x` must be named
```


:::
:::




## `.iter_walk()` and `.iter_iwalk()`

`.iter_map()` and `.iter_imap()` are for when you want the *results*.
`.iter_walk()` and `.iter_iwalk()` are their side-effect-only
counterparts: same iteration behaviour, but the return value is `.x`
itself, returned invisibly, so they compose neatly at the end of a
pipeline without cluttering the console with the results of every call
to `.f`:




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
.iter_walk(1:3, function(x) cat("value:", x, "\n"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
value: 1 
value: 2 
value: 3 
```


:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
.iter_iwalk(c(a = 1, b = 2), function(val, name) cat(name, "->", val, "\n"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
a -> 1 
b -> 2 
```


:::
:::




Because the input is returned invisibly, `.iter_walk()`/`.iter_iwalk()`
can be dropped into the middle of a longer expression purely for their
printing side effect, without changing what the expression evaluates
to:




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
result <- .iter_walk(1:3, function(x) cat("processing", x, "\n"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
processing 1 
processing 2 
processing 3 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
identical(result, 1:3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::
